# 5. Airport Slot Management

This chapter describes the standard interfaces for automatic management of airport slots.
The scope of these interfaces is the Ops Control system.
At some airports an airport slot is needed for any flight to depart or arrive. A slot is to be
seen as a contract between the airline and the airport, giving the airline the right to arrive
at and depart from an airport at a certain time of day with a certain aircraft type. The slot grants the
arrival/departure of the flight(s) within a specific time window. Stepping away from the agreed terms
means that the airline needs to follow a procedure which involves asking for permission to make a change
and waiting for the response.

Airport slot management is used at airports where demand is higher than capacity, at least during certain
times during the day, as a means to avoid congestion. Slot managed airports have a function called slot
coordinator (or slot facilitator) responsible for coordinating slots and communicate with airlines and
other stakeholders. The communication between JCMS and the slot coordinator uses standardized messages
described in Chapter 6 in the IATA SSIM Manual.

The Ops Control system keeps an up to date state of existing airport slots within a certain time window (current day + 3).
The time window is related to the operational time window and thus moves forward as time passes.
It is the task of the airport slot management services to retrieve existing slots from the slot
coordinator for all slot managed airports that are used by flights within the current time window. It
also detects situations that require new slot clearance requests and follows up on the response of such
requests.

## 5.1. Services

In JCMS, the following services are involved in the airport slot management process:

### 5.1.1. Slot Requests Output

This service is responsible for generating slot messages, sent from airline to airport slot coordinators.
The service finds relevant slot managed airports in JCMS within current slot window and sends requests to
slot coordinators of those airports for all existing slots within the slot window.
This service also fulfills the task of initiating the importing of allocated airport slots, when no slot information
yet exists in JCMS. Therefore no separate initial loading of slot information is needed.

The service generates the following type of slot messages:

SIR-Q (Slot Information Request Query):
The service sends SIR request messages to all slot managed airports each 6 hours. A SIR-Q message requests all slots
within the current slot window for a specific airport.
The service use Consul as a registry for storing the slot window associated with each sent SIR requests.

SCR/SMA (Slot Change Request):
The service performs continuous analysis of all airport slots within the current slot window, identifying those requiring changes.
SCR/SMA messages are then generated to airport coordinators for the concerned airport slots.
An airport slot requires a change when associated flight leg in JCMS has significantly changed (for example changed aircraft type or number of seats).
The business logic to determine whether a flight leg has significantly changed is airline specific and must be defined in the configuration layer, see Rave definitions.
The service also identifies airport slots where the associated flight leg has been cancelled, and no airport slot is required anymore.
Slots without any associated flight legs are currently not analyzed and managed by this service.
In terms of communication, SCR messages are generated for level 3 coordinated airports, whereas SMA messages are generated for level 2 coordinated airports.

5.1.1.1. Inconsistent state
The interface identifies situations where a user has saved temporary or intermediate changes to the aircraft rosters that
affects one or more slots. Changes to the affected slots are deferred and not sent to the slot coordinator until the state
of the model is deemed consistent. In an inconsistent state one or more slot coordinated flight legs have typically been
deassigned from the aircraft, however the inconsistent state may comprise not only the slots that are directly affected by
deassigned legs but additional slots may be indirectly affected due to aircraft swaps involving several aircraft.

5.1.1.2. Slot requests for new flights
The interface generates slot requests for new flights created from within JCMS as soon as they are assigned to an aircraft.
Slot requests are generated in accordance with the slot coordination level and slot type requirements at the flights departure
and arrival airport respectively.

### 5.1.2. Slot Response Input

This service is responsible for processing slot messages sent by airport slot coordinators to the airline,
updating the slot information in JCMS accordingly.
When processing slot messages, the service first tries to look up existing slot records in JCMS matching the
received slot information. The status (action code) of existing slots records in JCMS are updated to reflect the
new received information. New slot records are created in JCMS if no matching slot records are found.
The service also match flight legs in JCMS with the departure / arrival information of the received slot information and
associates the matching legs with the slot record in JCMS. Slot records are created in JCMS even if no matching flight legs are found.

The service can process the following type of slot message:

SIR (Slot Information Request):
It’s assumed that information in the received SIR response message corresponds with the slot window for the latest sent SIR-Q message for respective airport.
The service use Consul for looking up the latest requested SIR period and updates slot records in JCMS as a state,
meaning that existing slots are removed from JCMS if not included in the SIR response being processed.
Slots outside the latest requested SIR period are not processed or updated in JCMS.
The service use Consul as a registry for storing information that SIR response has been received.

SCR/SMA (Slot Change Request):
Updates the status (Confirmation, Refusal, Cancellation, Offer, etc.) for airport slots in JCMS
based on the information received from airport slot coordinator.

After consuming a message, the service also sends a message back to MRM in order to update MRM meta data about the slot message. Header property ‘mrm_msg_id’
on the incoming message is used to reference the message to update in MRM. The meta data includes information about the addressed airport and the service consuming
the message along with any error or warning messages. For SCR/SMA messages the meta data also includes information about flights involved.

## 5.2. Design

The slot management services are not defined using SMOG and thus no artifacts are built by the
IOService builder. Instead IOServer handlers and IOService configuration is provided in CARMSYS as
part of the Standard Interfaces component.

## 5.3. Configuration

### 5.3.1. Rave definitions

The following Rave variables are defined in the CARMSYS and used by the Airport Slot Management standard interface:

- interfaces_core.%leg_requires_departure_slot_request%: Returns true only when the flight leg requires a departure slot and the current slot associated with the flight leg departure must be changed though communication to airport coordinator with SCR/SMA message.
- interfaces_core.%leg_requires_departure_turnslot_request%: Returns true only when the flight leg requires a turn slot for departure and the current slot associated with the flight leg departure must be changed though communication to airport coordinator with SCR/SMA message.
- interfaces_core.%leg_requires_arrival_slot_request%: Returns true only when the flight leg requires an arrival slot for arrival and the current slot associated with the flight leg arrival must be changed though communication to airport coordinator with SCR/SMA message.
- interfaces_core.%leg_requires_arrival_turnslot_request%: Returns true only when the flight leg requires a turn slot for arrival and the current slot associated with the flight leg arrival must be changed though communication to airport coordinator with SCR/SMA message.
- interfaces_core.%leg_departure_airport_uses_turnslots%: Returns true if the departure airport of the flight leg uses turnslots as opposed to arrival/departure slots. This is used by the interface when requesting slots for new flights.
- interfaces_core.%leg_arrival_airport_uses_turnslots%: Returns true if the arrival airport of the flight leg uses turnslots as opposed to arrival/departure slots. This is used by the interface when requesting slots for new flights.

The business logic behind these Rave variables need to be implemented in a CARMUSR to comply with the
expected behavior of each individual airline.

### 5.3.2. Configuration of IOServer

IOServer need to be configured for hosting the interface IOServices:

&lt;include href=&quot;${CARMSYS}/etc/service_template/airport_slot_mgmt/AirportSlotRequests.xml&quot; /&gt;
&lt;include href=&quot;${CARMSYS}/etc/service_template/airport_slot_mgmt/AirportSlots.xml&quot; /&gt;

The following queues must be included in ccf configuration, typically located at $CARMUSR/etc/ccf.xml:

&lt;include href=&quot;${CARMSYS}/etc/ccf/airport_slot_mgmt.xml&quot;/&gt;

### 5.3.3. Infrastructure

Airport slot messages are communicated by email. The Slot Requests Output IOService is configured to forward
messages to Message Recipient Management (MRM) where per airport subscriptions are created for distributing
messages to email addresses of respective airport slot coordinator. MRM is also set up to read a mailbox
reserved for response messages from airport slot coordinators, and route those messages to the
Slot Response Input IOService.

# 6. API Hotels Integration

This chapter describes the interfaces that provides JCMS with an automated hotel accommodation process in cooperation with the external
crew accommodation provider Accommodations Plus International (API), providing airlines with services such as sourcing, negotiation, planning,
operations &amp; logistics, billing and analytics.

## 6.1. Overview of the business process

The integrated solution described here consists of a bidirectional exchange of information between JCT and the hotel booking system ACES from API.
It is designed to provide JCMS with a planned view of crew accommodations as well as responding to day of operation changes in order to keep the state of
hotel bookings automatically up-to-date and consistent with the actual air traffic situation, crew need etc. ACES always prioritizes responding to changes
to trips close to or on day of operation whereas changes to trips further out may be placed on queue to be picked up at a later date.

The data flowing in the direction from JCT to ACES serves the
purposes of communicating the need for hotel accommodation by sending the actual state of trips (pairings) and their assignments. When trips for the
upcoming planning period have been created in JCMS they are sent to ACES as a batch. Trips are completed with personal assignments as rosters are being
released for the various crew groups. Changes are then communicated to ACES in an on-event fashion, as the trips and rosters are maintained in JCMS.
In the same way, updates are also sent during the operational phase for assignment changes, flight cancellations, trip splits, flight delays and other
events that might affect the need for hotel accommodation or transportation to/from hotels or venues, as soon as changes are made in JCT. For the purpose
of booking local transportation to/from venues in ACES, venue information is included for ground tasks in the trip messages sent to ACES. Venue information
in this context is for example the location of a simulator or other training facilities.

The task of selecting actual hotels and room types based on the communicated need is essentially in the hands of ACES and is based on cost criteria,
availability as well as whatever other rules implemented in ACES for governing the choice of accommodation depending on crew, trip- or flight related properties.
It is the responsibility of ACES to fulfill the need for hotel accommodations at all times. However, JCT can also hint ACES about preferred hotels, specific
hotels requested by crew or special placeholders (so called forced hotels) for accommodation where a layover cannot be directly derived from the structure of
the trip, such as day rooms or need for hotel room at beginning or end of a trip. In addition to explicitly hinting ACES about the need for day rooms, ACES can
also be configured to automatically book day rooms for long stops.

JCT can also inform ACES about occasions where hotel or transport is not needed
for certain crew members due to private arrangements. Such arrangements may be initiated either from JCT or from ACES by means of the MyCrewCare mobile app.
In the latter case, information about declined hotel accommodation is sent over from ACES to JCT along with hotel bookings for the layover in question.

The data flow from ACES to JCT serves the purpose of providing JCMS with both a preliminary view of bookings as a response to the initial batch of
planned trips and to maintain an up-to-date state of bookings for JCMS as changes occur. Closer to day of operation, as roster assignments become available
and bookings are being confirmed by hotels, ACES sends confirmed personalized bookings to JCT. The communication around accommodation and transport need
as well as actual bookings is trip centric, i.e. both systems are using the trip concept as common planning object. As a consequence, so called non-crew
working on board the aircraft e.g. as technicians, air marshals or attending cargo, are normally not supported since they are not assigned to any of the
plannable crew positions of the trip. The trip name and IdentifierDate is used as a combined business key when trips are communicated between the systems.

Normally, all crew members on a certain trip have the same need for accommodation but it is not always the case.
Crew may be allocated different hotels e.g. for availability or contractual reasons.

Furthermore, despite the trip centric approach, individual crew requests as well as individual duty briefing times can still be communicated and taken into
account by ACES.

In addition to hotel rooms and local hotel/venue transportation, ACES can also create and maintain bookings for ground transport trip activities and send them
over to JCT. Furthermore there are also additional data feeds for keeping crew data, hotels, transport companies and other master data in synch between the
two systems. Hotels and transport companies and the associated contractual information is owned and mastered by ACES whereas crew and master data such as
bases, airports, duty codes and crew positions are mastered by JCT.

### 6.1.1. Synchronization of trips and bookings

There are two booking periods maintained in ACES, the current period containing trips that are currently being operated and a future period containing the planned
trips. The booking periods may align with the bid periods used at the airline. Another option is to use a rolling time window, for example 28 days, to define the
booking periods.

Trips and hotel bookings are always synchronized between JCT and ACES for the current booking period. Following steps describe how the next booking period is
planned and maintained. The exact process might differ for individual airlines, but the steps gives an idea of what a typical process could look like.

- Trips for next booking period are available in JCT. When and how trips are imported to JCT is airline specific and is not further described in this document.
- Trips are exported from JCT and loaded into ACES for the next booking period. All trips are loaded to ACES as a batch, providing the total layover need that is to be planned. This step is typically done about 20 days before the next booking period and can either be triggered manually or automatically from JCT.
- Planning is performed in ACES and hotels are assigned to the trips for the booking period. This step typically takes 5 days to finalize.
- Hotel bookings are automatically sent from ACES to JCT for the planned trips. The trips in JCT now have information of hotels booked for each layover.
- Crew are assigned to trips in JCT as part of the bidding / rostering process.
- Trips with crew assignments are exported from JCT to ACES for the next booking period. All trips are sent to ACES as a batch. This step is typically done about 7 days before start of next booking period. All changes to these trips are automatically sent from JCT to ACES after this point in time for keeping the booking period up to date.
- The booking period is maintained in ACES to match the trips and crew assignments received from JCT. Hotel bookings are updated in ACES and automatically communicated back to JCT. The picture below illustrates how trips and hotel bookings are synchronized between JCT and ACES for the next booking period at different points in time.

## 6.2. Design overview

### 6.2.1. Interfaces

The guiding design principle is that the two systems, JCT and ACES, should be loosely coupled and operate independently. Operations in the sending system should
not be affected if the receiving system is unable to handle or receive the sent messages. A number of interfaces is used for integrating the two systems:

Communication between the systems is asynchronous and stateless, where messages are exchanged in a publish/subscribe fashion. The responsibility of a
publishing system is to send messages on agreed channels. The responsibility of the subscribing system is to receive and handle the messages accordingly.
The receiving system is responsible for error handling related to the received messages. The two systems (ACES and JCT) can use API and Jeppesen infrastructure
for direct communication, but it is also possible to route the communication via the airlines infrastructure.

6.2.1.1. A1 Crew Info
The purpose of this interface is to keep ACES updated with the list of employees (crew members) for which hotel accommodations are managed. Non-crew are not included.
Crew data sent to ACES consist of crew member id (employee number), first and last name, gender, employments, home bases, aircraft qualifications, groups, positions
and hide periods.

Except from the crew member id, name and gender, all other record types sent over this interface come with a time validity, i.e. they can vary in time. For this kind
of data JCT tracks changes and stores the complete timeline i.e. current as well as historical and future data (if available). However the timeline sent to ACES
over this interface is by default limited to the current and next planning periods, i.e. from beginning of the current planning period until the end of the next
planning period.

The service produces messages on an internal interface format and then transforms them to the external ACES format by means of an xslt transformation (see Schemas, services and operations).

6.2.1.1.1. Hide periods
Hide periods are the combined periods of hold periods and unacknowledged periods for the crew member. This is communicated to ACES in order not to disclose information to crew
,e.g. from the MyCrewCare mobile app, about any assignments that may only be preliminary. In order for ACES to be able to react immediately to changes in hide periods,
e.g. as a result of crew acknowledging a roster change, crew data is sent on event-basis for crew as soon as there is a change in their hide periods.
In a customer installation, the Crew Info feed is also set up to run in a batch fashion in order to keep the rest of the crew data up-to-date and to make ACES aware
of any new crew members.

6.2.1.1.2. Translation of aircraft qualifications
Aircraft qualifications extracted from JCT are translated into fleet codes used by ACES. Since fleet codes in ACES are maximum 3 characters the aircraft qualifications
are by default translated into fleet codes by simply taking the 3 first characters of the qualification type code. This translation may need to be customized since
the naming scheme for qualification type codes may differ between airlines. Override method get_qual_id of class std_interfaces.api_hotels_1.CrewDataInterfaceHandler
in order to extract a custom fleet code based on an aircraft qualification.
Aircraft qualifications in JCT are recognized as crew qualifications having category code “aircraft”.

6.2.1.2. A2 Planned Pairings
The purpose of this interface is to export trips from JCT and load into ACES for the next booking period. All trips are loaded to ACES as a batch,
providing the total layover need that is to be planned. The feed comes in two flavors with similar content, the ‘Load-Pairings’ and the ‘Update-Pairings’ message
which both have very similar schema. When trips are initially created in JCMS, before they are known to ACES, JCT sends a Load-Pairings batch to ACES containing
the trips in open time. When rosters have been assigned, JCT sends an ‘Update-Pairings’ batch with the assigned trips. In a customer installation, the
Planned Pairings feed is set up to run in a batch fashion either by automatically scheduled jobs at certain dates of the month or to be manually initiated.

A trip must meet the following criteria to be sent to ACES:

- trip is not cancelled
- trip has a crew complement
- trip contains at least one activity
- trip is not a wrapper trip (category = ‘PRIV_TASK’) containing only one activity

The service produces messages on an internal interface format and then transforms them to the external ACES format by means of an xslt transformation (see Schemas, services and operations).

6.2.1.2.1. Special layover requests
Normally, API Hotels derives the need for accommodation based on the state of the trips and makes reservations according to booking rules in ACES. However, this
interface is also able to convey various requests along with the trips. ACES will use such requests as input in the booking process and try to accommodate them
if possible. Note that the types of special requests listed here also apply to interface A3 Pairing/Roster Updates. As an example, if a request for a certain
hotel has been placed on a trip, that request is included in the trip state and thus included in (A2 or A3) messages to ACES, containing that trip.

Requests may be on trip level or roster level. Trip level requests apply to all crew/positions of the trip, whereas roster level requests only apply to specified
crew members. Trip level requests may be combined with roster level requests either to make exceptions to a trip level request for certain crew member(s), or to
add properties to a trip level request for individual crew member(s). As an example, a hotel specified in a trip level request is overridden by another hotel
for a certain crew member as specified in a roster level request. See also Use cases for an example of a trip level request.

where decline of accommodation is initiated from ACES (by means of the MyCrewCare app), the A6 interface does not distinguish between decline of room vs. transports.
Therefore one roster_event of each type (SKIP_ROOM, SKIP_TO_HOTEL and SKIP_FROM_HOTEL) is created. See also Handling of declined hotel accommodations.

6.2.1.2.2. Message header attributes
The following headers attributes are attached to each message sent over interfaces A2 and A3:

current_pp - Set to ‘True’ if the message contains trips with IdentifierDate that are within the range of the current planning period, else ‘False’.

next_pp - Set to ‘True’ if the message contains trips with IdentifierDate that are within the range of the next planning period, else ‘False’.

A planning period ‘pp’ is defined as the period between two points in time tStart and tEnd, i.e. tStart &lt;= t &lt; tEnd.

The logic to determine if a trip IdentifierDate ‘d’ is within the range of a planning period ‘pp’ is to compare ‘d’ with the date part of tStart and tEnd, i.e.
date(tStart) &lt;= d &lt;date(tEnd).

Example 1,
Message containing trips with IdentifierDate between 1NOV2020 and 1DEC2020
current planning period: 1OCT2020 00:00 - 1NOV2020 00:00
next planning period: 1NOV2020 00:00 - 1DEC2020 0:00
result: ‘current_pp’ = ‘False’, ‘next_pp’ = ‘True’

Example 2,
Message containing trips with IdentifierDate between 1FEB2020 and 28FEB2020
current planning period: 1FEB2020 08:00 - 1MAR2020 08:00
next planning period: 1MAR2020 08:00 - 1APR2020 08:00
result: ‘current_pp’ = ‘True’, ‘next_pp’ = ‘False’

Example 3,
Message containing trips with IdentifierDate between 1FEB2020 and 15MAR2020
current planning period: 1FEB2020 08:00 - 1MAR2020 08:00
next planning period: 1MAR2020 08:00 - 1APR2020 08:00
result: ‘current_pp’ = ‘True’, ‘next_pp’ = ‘True’

6.2.1.2.3. Deadheads and Sick Transports
Information whether a flight leg is used by the airline for positioning crew due to deadheading or sick transport, is forwarded to ACES to allow for business logic
with special considerations or arrangements.

6.2.1.3. A3 Pairing/Roster Updates
The purpose of this interface is to keep ACES up to date with changes to trips and their activities (segments) and assigned crew, close to and during day of operation.
Changed trips are identified by a trigger service in JCT and sent with their new state, one message per trip. Although conceptually different from the batch feeds
described above in A2 Planned Pairings, the trip state information sent for a trip is the same.

The following types of changes are picked up by the trigger:

- trip split operations
- trip slice operations
- new trips
- removed trips
- cancelled trips
- activities added to trip
- activities removed from trip
- changes to duty overrides
- schedule time or venue changes of ground activities
- changes of scheduled, estimated or actual times of flights
- changes to hotel requests both on trip and on the individual crew level
- changes to crew declines of hotel accommodations and transports
- changes to forced hotels both on trip level and for individual crew members
- changes to briefing time overrides both on trip level and for individual crew members
- changes in aircraft assignments
- trips becoming released for crew members
- changes to crew-trip assignments

In addition to these trip related changes, the trigger also identifies situations where a trip that is de-assigned from a roster overlaps another trip on the same
roster. In this case both trips are sent to ACES regardless if the latter trip is subject to any of the above changes or not.

Messages are not sent for changes to trips in historic time. By default, changes to trips ending more than 5 days ago are not sent. Furthermore, the trip must meet
the following criteria to be sent to ACES:

- trip is not cancelled
- trip has a crew complement
- trip contains at least one activity
- trip is not a wrapper trip (category = ‘PRIV_TASK’) containing only one activity

The service produces messages on an internal interface format and then transforms them to the external ACES format by means of an xslt transformation (see also Schemas, services and operations).
The trigger picks up changes at discrete times following the so called model refresh interval in the IOServer. The trigger creates a ‘TripEventsMsg’ message on the
internal interface format containing all changes in one change-set, i.e. changes that occurred since the last model refresh. The ‘TripEventsMsg’ is then transformed
into multiple messages on the external ACES formats.

6.2.1.3.1. Event messages sent to ACES
There are specific messages sent for trip cancellations ‘Delete-Pairing’, assignment changes ‘Assign-Pairing’, and new trips ‘Add-Pairing’. All other events
are communicated using the ‘Revise-Pairing’ message. For trip slice and split operations, the ‘Revise-Pairing’ message contains both trips resulting from the
operation. If a trip is subject to several changes, more than one of these message types may be sent. The interface then guarantees that the messages are sent in
a logical order. The ‘Add-Pairing’ and ‘Revise-Pairing’ messages contain the full state of the trip including their crew assignments. Therefore if e.g. a trip
has been created and assigned in the same transaction then the ‘Assign-Pairing’ is redundant and only the ‘Add-Pairing’ message is sent.
For the ‘Assign-Pairing’ message, even though it only contains the trip key and crew assignments, always contains the full state of assignments. I.e. if a crew
member has been de-assigned from a trip, the message contains all the remaining crew assignments. See Schemas, services and operations for the schemas of these messages.

6.2.1.3.2. Message header attributes
The following headers attributes are attached to each message sent over interfaces A2 and A3:

current_pp - Set to ‘True’ if the message contains trips with IdentifierDate that are within the range of the current planning period, else ‘False’.

next_pp - Set to ‘True’ if the message contains trips with IdentifierDate that are within the range of the next planning period, else ‘False’.

A planning period ‘pp’ is defined as the period between two points in time tStart and tEnd, i.e. tStart &lt;= t &lt; tEnd.

The logic to determine if a trip IdentifierDate ‘d’ is within the range of a planning period ‘pp’ is to compare ‘d’ with the date part of tStart and tEnd, i.e.
date(tStart) &lt;= d &lt;date(tEnd).

Note that the ‘Revise-Pairing’ message is also sent as a response to a ‘Request-Pairing-Refresh’ message sent by ACES to query for trip state of individual
trips (see A4 Request Pairing Request).

6.2.1.3.3. Incident lock
An incident lock flag, that a flight leg may be tagged with in JCT, is forwarded to ACES in order for API Hotels to restrict access to information related to such
a flight leg.

6.2.1.3.4. Deadheads and Sick Transports
Information whether a flight leg is used by the airline for positioning crew due to deadheading or sick transport, is forwarded to ACES to allow for business logic
with special considerations or arrangements.

6.2.1.3.5. Additional duty information
By adding a Hotel Option comment on a certain layover in a trip, a crew tracker in JCT can convey information about special arrangements to ACES. Such information
and arrangements are agreed between the airline and API Hotels on a project implementation basis. An example could be special pickup locations for charter flights.
The information is stored in JCT as a trip_event of type HOTEL_OVERRIDE and transferred by the interface as a duty remark. Should more than one such trip_event
exist for the same trip layover, all comments are concatenated and comma-separated into one duty remark.

6.2.1.4. A4 Request Pairing Request
The purpose of this interface is to give ACES the possibility to query JCT for the current trip state for individual trips or all trips within a period.
It is mainly used for recovering from out-of-synch issues that may occur due to outages, missed messages etc, but can also be useful when testing
the system integration. Communication is asynchronous, where a request message is published from ACES to JCT and a response message is published back from
JCT to ACES on interface A3 Pairing/Roster Updates or A2 Planned Pairings depending on request type (see below).

Request messages are sent on an external ACES format and transformed into an internal format by means of an xslt transformation. Response messages are also
produced on an internal interface format and transformed into the external ACES format. See also Schemas, services and operations for more information.
Depending on the request type, JCT responds with different types of response messages:

- Request type “list-of-pairings” yields one or more messages of type Revise-Pairing (see A3 Pairing/Roster Updates)
- Request type “range-request” yields one message of type Update-Pairings (see A2 Planned Pairings)
- Request type “list-of-bases” is ignored by JCT.

6.2.1.5. A5 Hotel Data Export
The purpose of this interface is to load and update JCT with information about hotels and transportation companies (TC) used for accommodating and transporting
crew members on layovers. This information is needed in JCMS primarily for crew control to know how to contact crew on the layover. The list of hotels and TCs
are also used in JCT for crew trackers to select hotels when requesting specific hotels. The information (including rates and other hotel contract details) may
also be used by the pairing/tracking optimizers for finding overall optimal scheduling solutions.

In a customer installation, the Hotel Data Export feed is normally set up to run in a batch fashion on a nightly basis. As a complement, the feed may also be set
up to run on an event basis, exporting new or modified hotels or TCs as soon as they are added/modified in ACES. If e.g. a hotel booking is received for a hotel
that is not yet known to JCT, the hotel is created ad-hoc with temporary limited information. The information about the hotel is then limited to name,
address and phone number until the hotel becomes available in the Hotel Data Export feed. The interface also creates a record in airport_hotel associating
the layover station with the newly created hotel.

Only hotels and transportation companies included in a message from ACES are created/updated in JCT. Hotels and transport companies that exist in JCT but are
not included in the feed are not deleted in JCT by the interface. JCT is informed about hotels and transportation companies no longer in use through the validity
period of their contracts.

Messages are sent on an external ACES format and transformed into an internal format by means of an xslt transformation (see also Schemas, services and operations).

6.2.1.6. A6 Pairing Hotel Details
The purpose of this interface is to keep JCMS up to date with information about what hotels and transports that are planned/booked/confirmed for each layover and crew
member. This information is required in JCMS primarily for crew control to know that all crew have accommodations and transports for the layovers and how crew can be
contacted if needed, but also for crew members to know what hotels and transport companies that have been allocated for them.

Messages are sent on an external ACES format and transformed into an internal format by means of an xslt transformation (see also Schemas, services and operations).

The information sent over this interface is trip centric i.e. hotel and transport bookings are reported and managed per trip. One or more trips can be reported per
message and for each trip the complete state of bookings are always reported. This means for a certain trip bookings are always included for all layovers and all
positions of the trip. A consequence of the trip centric approach is also that ACES sends new booking status also in cases where trips are sliced or split without
changing the actual need for accommodations. As an example, slicing a trip results in a part of the booking need being shifted from the original trip to the new
resulting trip. While the total booking need remains the same (and thus the hotel reservations remain unchanged), there is a change in the state of bookings seen
from the trip perspective, therefore ACES must report the new booking states for the original trip and the new resulting trip.

The interface supports the following functional features:

- anonymous bookings (for open positions)
- personal bookings (for assigned crew members)
- crew members split to multiple hotels on the same layover
- bookings for layover before first duty of the trip
- bookings for layover after last duty of the trip
- dayroom bookings
- booking status per individual hotel reservations
- multi-night layovers
- multiple venue transport bookings during multi-night layovers to/from hotel
- information about crew members with declined hotel
- check-in/out times
- transport pickup times

6.2.1.6.1. Matching of existing booking records
Because ACES sends the complete state of bookings for a trip, in many situations the message will contain information that has not changed compared to the state
of bookings already in JCT. In order to cause as few updates as possible, the interface identifies what differs and updates only those records in the JCT database.

When receiving reservations for a certain trip layover from ACES, the interface first tries to match the given start and end times of the layover with the trip’s
Rave calculated duty start and end times, or activity start/end times in case of dayrooms (in this context it should also be pointed out that reservations for
multi-night layovers span over more than one duty). These duty (or activity) times must match exactly. If a match is not found, the default
behaviour in JCT is to ignore the reservation. It can generally be assumed that such mismatches are of temporary nature and are caused by trips being rebuilt in
JCT or by considerable delays of flights. When the trip has been updated in ACES, the new booking state sent should then match the trip in JCT.

If the reservation is deemed to match the trip, the interface tries to find an existing hotel_booking record to reuse. It first looks among previously handled
bookings to see if there is an exact match that can be reused. An exact match is one that matches not only start/end times, station and hotel but also transport
companies, booking status, check-in/out and pickup times. This is the case when ACES reports the same layover in separate &lt;layover&gt; or &lt;accomodation&gt; elements for
different crew members.

If no candidate was found the interface then tries to find an existing hotel_booking record that best matches the given hotel reservation. It is checked that the
selected candidate has not already been associated with some other reservation in the message. If a matching record is still not found a new hotel_booking is
created.

Based on the hotel_booking record, the interface then tries to find an existing trip_event record to reuse (or one per layover night in case of multi-night
layover), first among the trip_event records referencing the hotel_booking record and secondly among other trip_event records associated with the trip.
If no match is found a new trip_event record is created with a reference to the hotel_booking record.

When booking records have been created/updated as needed, personal bookings are matched and created if needed for any crew members associated with the reservation
from ACES. Any obsolete crew_hotel_booking records are deleted (as needed e.g. following a crew swap). Also the cnt and grouped_cnt columns of the
hotel_booking are updated to reflect the booked crew members.

6.2.1.6.2. Handling of intermediate booking states
An intermediate booking state arises in the JCT data model when a change has been done in JCT that will affect the (trip centric) view of bookings, but JCT has
not yet received reservations from ACES that reflect the new state. Some operations, e.g. slicing or splitting a trip, may leave previously confirmed
bookings with an undefined status, in the intermediate booking state. The interface can detect this situation when a hotel_booking record is handled, by looking at
the trip(s) referencing that hotel_booking. If it is no longer referenced by the trip it was once created for, it indicates that the original trip has been split. The interface
then updates the hotel_booking status to “New” indicating that a new state update from ACES is pending. Note that the column booking_ref holds a “soft
reference” to the trip for which the booking was created. This value of booking_ref remains for as long as the intermediate booking state lasts. In the “final”
booking state, after receiving notifications from ACES that reflect the new state, booking_ref refers to the new trip segment.

In the case of slicing a trip, all trip_event records refering to the original trip are cloned and the new clones are associated with the new trip slice.
This happens as an integral part of the slice operation in JCT and leaves the data model in an intermediate state where the existing booking records are referenced
both from the original trip and the new trip slice. In this case the interface clones the hotel_booking records so that each booking is only referenced from
one trip_event. The booking status is set to “New” for the booking records associated with a trip for which notifications has not yet arrived from ACES.

For more information see ‘Splitting and slicing a trip’ in Use cases.

6.2.1.6.3. Handling of cancelled bookings
ACES does not support sending cancelled bookings. However when an updated booking state is received from ACES, any non-matching hotel_booking records that may
exist already in the JCT database are updated with status “CANCELLED”. This way bookings are implicitly cancelled in JCT. Any trip_event records referencing
the cancelled hotel_booking records are deleted, unless they also belong to another trip. Any crew_hotel_booking records referencing the cancelled
hotel_booking are also removed.

6.2.1.6.4. Handling of declined hotel accommodations
In the case where decline of accommodation is initiated from ACES (by means of the MyCrewCare app), the interface does not distinguish between decline of room vs.
transports. Therefore one roster_event of each type (SKIP_ROOM, SKIP_TO_HOTEL and SKIP_FROM_HOTEL) is created. The interface also adds ‘EXT API Hotels’ as
remark in order to distinguish them from declines initiated from JCT. This is important in order for the interface to correctly identify the case where a previous
decline in MyCrewCare has been removed, and thus to prevent the interface from removing roster_event records initiated from JCT, e.g. created in the Tracking
Editor.

6.2.1.7. A7 Request Hotel Request
The purpose of this interface is to give JCT the possibility to query ACES for the current state of hotel and transport bookings.
It may be used for recovering from out-of-synch issues e.g. due to outages, missed messages etc, but can also be useful when testing
the system integration. Communication is asynchronous, where a request message is published from JCT to ACES and a response message is published back from
ACES to JCT on interface A6 Pairing Hotel Details. There are two types of requests available, by trip or by roster (by specifying employee number and period).

Request messages are sent on an external ACES format. Response messages are produced on an external ACES format and transformed into the internal interface
format. See also Schemas, services and operations for more information.

This interface is available on a configuration basis, if deemed necessary by a customer implementation project. There is no built-in feature in JCT for issuing
request messages of this kind.

6.2.1.8. A8 Transport Bookings
The purpose of this interface is to keep JCT up to date with booking information for ground transportations between airports/cities made in ACES.
Ground transportations, for example taxi or limo activities, are sent to ACES as trip duty ground segment activities on interface A2 Planned Pairings or
A3 Pairing/Roster Updates. API Hotels may arrange the bookings of such ground transports and send transport booking details back to JCT.
The transport booking details is primarily required in JCMS for crew members to know what transport company that provides the transport.

Booking messages are sent from ACES when transport bookings are created or updated. Messages are sent on an external ACES format and transformed into an internal
format by means of an xslt transformation (see also Schemas, services and operations).
The internal interface is the same as the one used for hotel bookings (see A6 Pairing Hotel Details).

For each booking, the interface creates a public annotation on the ground transport activity in the data model, containing the name and phone number of the
transport provider. The correct ground transport activity object is found by matching the given start and end stations, and ‘fuzzy’ matching of the given start and
end times against existing ground transports assigned to the given trip. If several candidates are found within the allowed deviation (default 60 minutes), the one
closest in time is picked. The interface writes ‘EXT API Hotels’ in the ‘created_by’ field of the annotation in order to recognize it as a ground transport booking
annotation, in case there are other public annotations associated with a certain ground transport. If a ground transport booking annotation already exists, the
interface updates the annotation text and the ‘creation_time’ if the provider name or phone number has changed.

6.2.1.9. J1 Static Data
The purpose of this interface is to simplify and standardize the import of static data from JCT into ACES and keep the static data in ACES up to date with changes
in JCT. This interface consists of two feeds for different types of static data (a.k.a. master data or catalog data), the ‘AirportDataValidity’ and the
‘CatalogDataOutput’. In a customer installation, the ‘CatalogDataOutput’ feed is typically set up to run in a batch fashion once per night whereas the latest
version of the airport data is always available as an xml file to download from Jeppesen Plaza.

The ‘AirportDataValidity’ message contains the following types of master data:

- airports
- time zones
- daylight saving time patterns
- cities
- countries
- country subdivisions
- regions

The ‘CatalogDataOutput’ message contains the following types of master data:

- airlines
- crew bases
- crew groups and categories
- qualification groups and categories
- seniority groups
- planning periods
- activity (duty) types, groups and categories
- aircraft types, groups and body types
- flight service types
- currencies
- coterminals
- trip categories
- gender codes

Note that for this interface there doesn’t exist any external ACES format. ACES consumes Jeppesen interface formats for these feeds (see also Schemas, services and operations).
For more details on these feeds please see Airport Data Input and Catalog data output.

### 6.2.3. Data Model

The picture below shows the portion of the data model most relevant for the API Hotels Integration. Details have been left out for clarity and only primary key
columns and selected external references have been included. Please refer to the UDM documentation for more details. Also see Use cases for
examples of how the data model is used by the interfaces.

As can be seen from the picture, there are actually two tables that can hold hotel and transport bookings - trip_event and hotel_booking.
While hotel_booking reflects the actual bookings as received from ACES, trip_event represents a “best known” state of bookings which means either an “intended”
hotel allocation or the actual bookings. There are also other uses for the trip_event table in the context of hotel bookings, e.g. to indicate “forced hotels” or
requests for specific hotel. The type of trip_event is determined by the referenced plan_event_type.

The trip_event records always represent a single layover night on a certain trip. Multi-night layovers are mapped to several trip_event records, one per night,
but only one hotel_booking record (see also Multi-night layovers). The individual trip_event records therefore reference the same
hotel_booking, which then covers the total multi-night layover length.
There may also be more than one instance of trip_event/hotel_booking per layover night e.g. in case crew are split up on different hotels or different transport
companies. In those cases the grouped_cnt shows number of crew and positions for each booking.

In contrast to trip_event, roster_event never represent bookings. In the context of hotel bookings it is only used to indicate “forced hotels”, requests
for specific hotel or declined hotel or transport for individual crew members. Personal hotel and transport bookings are represented by the crew_hotel_booking
table.

The dashed line from hotel_booking to trip in the figure represents a “soft reference” to the trip for which the booking was created, stored in column booking_ref.

### 6.2.4. Booking statuses

The following booking status codes are used in the API Hotels integration.

JCT status

ACES status

Description

BOOKED

BOOKED

Booking is confirmed.

CANCELLED

CANCELLED

Booking is cancelled.

PENDING_CONFIRM

PENDING CONFIRMATION

Rooms have been reserved but not confirmed by hotel.

PENDING_CANCEL

PENDING CANCELLATION

Cancellation is initiated but has not been confirmed by the hotel.

New

Booking is in an intermediate state. This status is initiated from JCT, there is no corresponding
corresponding status sent by ACES.

The interface can be configured to ignore certain booking statuses from ACES. By default, status codes “PENDING CANCELLATION” and “CANCELLED” are ignored by JCT.
For more information about cancelled bookings and the New status see Handling of cancelled bookings and Handling of intermediate booking states.

### 6.2.5. Multi-night layovers

Multi-night layovers are represented by several trip_event records, one per night, but only one hotel_booking record. However multi-night bookings may also be
associated with multiple transportations to/from hotel or venues in which case more than one hotel_booking record is needed in order to correctly model all
associated transports. In this case all of the hotel_booking records have the same start/end time reflecting the total length of the multi-night layover.

The first layover night is assumed to have a transport from airport to hotel whereas the last layover night is assumed to have an associated transport from hotel to
airport. In case of multiple transports, intermediate layover nights may also have transports from venue to hotel and/or from hotel to venue.
A venue is for example the location of a simulator or other training facilities associated with a ground duty. Based on the specified transport pickup times the
interface tries to associate each transport with the correct layover.

### 6.3.2. Integrator Camel routes and queue names

The infrastructure described here assumes that communication with ACES is done via an external ActiveMQ broker (refered to as externalBroker in the Camel route
configuration snippets below). Queue names should be reviewed in cooperation with API Hotels on a project configuration basis. The internal ActiveMQ queue names
basically match with those generated as IOServices configuration templates by the IOService builder based on the configuration
in IOService builder and IOServer configuration. However, for interfaces having both a batch and an on-event output, the sinks should be directed to a

&lt;route id=&quot;export_CrewDataHotel_1_plainxml&quot;&gt;
  &lt;from uri=&quot;internalBroker:queue:{{env:CCF_PREFIX}}from.ioservice.CrewDataHotel_1_plainxml&quot; /&gt;
  &lt;to uri=&quot;bean:LogMetrics&quot; /&gt;
  &lt;to uri=&quot;bean:FilehubReadAsStream&quot; /&gt;

&lt;/route&gt;

&lt;route id=&quot;CrewDataHotel_1_plainxml_error&quot;&gt;
  &lt;from uri=&quot;internalBroker:queue:{{env:CCF_PREFIX}}from.ioservice.CrewDataHotel_1_plainxml.error&quot; /&gt;
  &lt;to uri=&quot;bean:LogMetrics?method=error&quot; /&gt;

&lt;/route&gt;

6.3.2.2. Interface A2, A3 and A4 - Trip data sent to ACES
&lt;route id=&quot;export_CrewOnTripHotel_1_plainxml&quot;&gt;
  &lt;from uri=&quot;internalBroker:queue:{{env:CCF_PREFIX}}from.ioservice.CrewOnTripHotel_1_plainxml&quot; /&gt;
  &lt;to uri=&quot;bean:LogMetrics&quot; /&gt;
  &lt;to uri=&quot;bean:FilehubReadAsStream&quot; /&gt;
    &lt;convertBodyTo type=&quot;java.lang.String&quot;/&gt;
    &lt;removeHeaders pattern=&quot;JMS_AMQP*&quot;/&gt;
    &lt;choice&gt;
        &lt;!-- Messages should be routed to current/next queue according to header attributes. --&gt;
        &lt;when&gt;
            &lt;simple&gt;${header[JMSType]} == &amp;quot;Load-Pairings&amp;quot;&lt;/simple&gt;
            &lt;to pattern=&quot;InOnly&quot; uri=&quot;externalBroker:queue:JCMS.V1.JMS.ACES_OPS_NEXT_PAIRINGS_OUTBOUND&quot;/&gt;
        &lt;/when&gt;
        &lt;when&gt;
            &lt;simple&gt;${header[current_pp]} == &amp;quot;True&amp;quot;&lt;/simple&gt;
            &lt;to pattern=&quot;InOnly&quot; uri=&quot;externalBroker:queue:JCMS.V1.JMS.ACES_OPS_CURRENT_PAIRINGS_OUTBOUND&quot;/&gt;
        &lt;/when&gt;
        &lt;when&gt;
            &lt;simple&gt;${header[next_pp]} == &amp;quot;True&amp;quot;&lt;/simple&gt;
            &lt;to pattern=&quot;InOnly&quot; uri=&quot;externalBroker:queue:JCMS.V1.JMS.ACES_OPS_NEXT_PAIRINGS_OUTBOUND&quot;/&gt;
        &lt;/when&gt;
        &lt;otherwise&gt;
            &lt;to pattern=&quot;InOnly&quot; uri=&quot;externalBroker:queue:JCMS.V1.JMS.ACES_OPS_NEXT_PAIRINGS_OUTBOUND&quot;/&gt;
        &lt;/otherwise&gt;
    &lt;/choice&gt;
    &lt;toD uri=&quot;msglog:${routeId}:file:{{env:INTEGRATOR_LOG_MSG_DIR}}&quot;/&gt;
  &lt;to uri=&quot;bean:FilehubDelete&quot; /&gt;
&lt;/route&gt;

&lt;route id=&quot;CrewOnTripHotel_1_plainxml_error&quot;&gt;
  &lt;from uri=&quot;internalBroker:queue:{{env:CCF_PREFIX}}from.ioservice.CrewOnTripHotel_1_plainxml.error&quot; /&gt;
  &lt;to uri=&quot;bean:LogMetrics?method=error&quot; /&gt;
  &lt;to uri=&quot;bean:FilehubReadAsStream&quot; /&gt;
  &lt;toD uri=&quot;msglog:CrewOnTripHotel_1_plainxml:file:{{env:INTEGRATOR_LOG_MSG_DIR}}?logAlways=true&amp;amp;suffix=error&quot; /&gt;
  &lt;to uri=&quot;bean:FilehubDelete&quot; /&gt;
&lt;/route&gt;

### 6.3.3. Rave Definitions

The following Rave variables are defined in the CARMSYS and used by the API Hotels interfaces:

- interfaces_core.%trip_out_duty_layover_station%: Defines duty layover station.
- interfaces_core.%duty_sched_start_utc%: Defines the scheduled duty start time in UTC, excluding briefing time if any.
- interfaces_core.%duty_sched_end_utc%: Defines the scheduled duty end time in UTC, excluding debriefing time if any.
- interfaces_core.%next_duty_sched_start_utc%: Defines the scheduled duty start time of next duty in UTC, excluding briefing time if any.
- interfaces_core.%next_duty_sched_end_utc%: Defines the scheduled duty end time of next duty in UTC, excluding debriefing time if any.
- interfaces_core.%duty_is_first_in_trip%: True if duty is first in trip.
- interfaces_core.%duty_is_last_in_trip%: True if duty is last in trip.
- interfaces_core.%duty_start_station%: Defines the station at start of the duty.
- interfaces_core.%duty_end_station%: Defines the station at end of the duty.
- interfaces_core.%leg_sched_end_utc%: Defines the scheduled end time of the activity in UTC.
- interfaces_core.%leg_end_station%: Defines the end station of the activity.
- interfaces_core.%next_leg_sched_start_utc%: Defines the scheduled start time of the next activity in UTC.
- interfaces_core.%leg_is_sick_transport%: True if flight is assigned for sick transport.
- interfaces_core.%requested_hotel_id_after_duty%: If not void, provides a ‘default’ requested hotel for a layover.
- interfaces_core.%api_hotels_estimated_time_threshold%: If not void, specifies the number of minutes estimated times must change in JCT for sending update messages to ACES.

The business logic behind these Rave variables need to be implemented in a CARMUSR to comply with the expected behavior of each individual airline.

### 6.3.5. Tenant specific schemas

If the external (ACES) schemas need to be extended as part of the airline specific configuration, API Hotels should release schemas with an airline
specific target namespace, e.g. http://ws.apihotels.com/transactions/v1/NZ/v1.
Airline specific schemas should be placed in $CARMUSR/data/config/smog/v2/api_hotels_1/schema using the original names (see Schemas, services and operations).
If airline specific xslt transform stylesheets are required, they should likewise be placed in this directory under their original names.
Interfaces look for schemas and stylesheets first in this directory and if not found there they fall back to $CARMSYS/data/config/smog/v2/api_hotels_1/schema.
The custom target namespace, as specified by the ‘targetNamespace’ attribute is automatically used by outbound interfaces when creating messages to be sent to ACES.

## 6.4. Trouble shooting

### 6.4.1. Error messages

All errors are logged by the IOServices with loglevel ERROR in the log file of the respective IOServer that hosts the service, e.g. errors from service
LayoverInput are logged in $CARMTMP/logfiles/ioserver_single1.log. Errors reported by inbound services are generally fatal and result in discarding of the
processed message.

### 6.4.2. Logging

In addition to error messages, there are also a number of situations where messages are logged with loglevels WARNING and INFO:

Interface

Level

Message

Comment

A6

INFO

Ignored reservation for non-matching layover. Trip: {ref}
layover: {from} - {to} at {stn} hotel {id} for crew {id}

A booking from ACES doesn’t match the trip, and option
ignore_unknown_layovers = True.

A6

INFO

Ignored reservation for non-matching layover before or
after trip: {ref} layover: {from} - {to} at {stn} hotel
{id} for crew {id}

A booking from ACES for a layover before or after the trip
doesn’t match the trip, and option
ignore_unknown_layovers = True.

A6

INFO

Created trip_event for trip {ref}, non-matching layover:
{from} - {to} at {stn} hotel {id}

A trip_event was created for a booking from ACES that doesn’t
match the trip, because option
ignore_unknown_layovers = False.

A6

INFO

Created trip_event for trip {ref}, layover: {from} - {to}
at {stn} hotel {id}

A trip_event was created for a booking from ACES that matches
the trip.

A6

INFO

Created hotel_booking for transport information related to
layover night {from}-{to} for trip {ref}, multi-night
layover: {from} - {to} at {stn} hotel {id} for crew {id}

Created a copy of the hotel_booking record to store transport info
specific to an individual layover night in a multi-night layover.

A6

INFO

Removed obsolete trip_event for trip {ref}, {layover type}
layover: {from} - {to} at {stn} hotel {id}

Detected and rempved unused trip_event record.

A2,A3

WARNING

No duty found for crew {id} assigned to trip {ref} for
duty starting with activity {ref} and ending with activity
{ref}

No Rave duty was found on crew members roster that matches
the trip duty chain. The interface is unable to handle any
hotel overrides associated with this crew member.

A6

INFO

Ignored {booking status} reservation. Trip: {ref} layover:
{from} - {to} at {stn} hotel {id} for crew {id}

Booking from ACES ignored because booking status should be
ignored according to option ignore_states.

A6

INFO

Created hotel_booking for {booking status} reservation for
trip {ref}, {layover type} layover: {from} - {to} at {stn}
hotel {id} for crew {id}

Created a hotel_booking record for a booking from ACES.

A6

WARNING

Trip does not exist: dor={trip_date} name={trip_name}

ACES sent a booking for a trip that does not exist in JCT plan.

A6

WARNING

Crew {id} not found

ACES sent a booking for a crew that does not exist in JCT plan.
Booking is still processed and any existing crew are booked.

A6

WARNING

Booking {before/after} trip {ref} missing forced layover
event on trip level.

ACES sent a booking for a layover before/after the trip but no
corresponding FORCED_HOTEL trip_event was found (expects layover
forced on trip level since trip is in open time). Booking from
ACES for this layover is ignored.

A6

WARNING

Booking {before/after} trip {ref} missing forced layover
event on trip or roster level

ACES sent a booking for a layover before/after the trip but no
corresponding FORCED_HOTEL trip_event nor roster_event was found.
Booking from ACES for this layover is ignored.

A6

INFO

Dayroom booking initiated by ACES for trip {ref} between
‘{act}’ and ‘{act}’

ACES sent a booking for a dayroom and no corresponding
FORCED_HOTEL trip_event or roster_event was found, indicating that
the reservation was initiated by a long stop booking rule in ACES.

A6

INFO

Removed duplicate referenced trip_event for trip {ref},
layover: {from} - {to} at {stn} hotel {id}

While looking for existing trip_event for a booking from ACES:
Identified and removed duplicate trip_event.

A2,A3,A6

INFO

Removed duplicate trip_event for trip {ref}, layover:
{from} - {to} at {stn} hotel {id}

Identified and removed what appeared to be an obsolete duplicate
trip_event.

A6

INFO

Removed trip_event for trip {ref}, layover: {from} - {to}
at {stn} hotel {id} while handling orphan bookings.

While handling orphan bookings: Detected and removed trip_event
connected to an obsolete booking.

A6

INFO

Created hotel_booking clone with ‘New’ status for trip
{ref}, layover: {from} - {to} at {stn} hotel {id} for crew
{id}

While handling a transient booking state: Created a clone of the
booking and associated trip_events with the new clone. See also
Handling of intermediate booking states.

A6

INFO

Removed trip_event for trip {ref}, layover: {from} - {to}
at {stn} hotel {id}.

While handling obsolete bookings: Detected and removed trip_event
connected to an obsolete booking.

A6

INFO

Cancelled hotel_booking for trip {ref}, layover: {from}
{to} at {stn} hotel {id} for crew {id} at {stn} hotel {id}

While handling obsolete bookings: Marked obsolete hotel_booking
as cancelled.

A5

WARNING

Ignoring contract for hotel with id ‘{id}’ due to invalid
contract period validfrom={from}, validto={to}

Invalid hotel contract period, validto &gt;= validfrom.

A5

WARNING

Ignoring contract for hotel transport company with id
‘{id}’ due to invalid contract period
validfrom={from}, validto={to}.

Invalid hotel transport company contract period,
validto &gt;= validfrom.

### 6.5.3. Forced hotel after trip

This scenario illustrates a case where a layover is forced after the trip, and the trip is in open time. In addition to just requesting a placeholder for the
extra layover, there is also a request for a specific hotel to be booked. The id of the requested hotel in this example is 222.
Note that in reality, the use case for forcing a layover after a trip is normally to keep already existing bookings in trip split scenarios. However for the sake of
simplicity, the example shown here does not involve a trip split.

### 6.5.4. Multi-night layover

A series of ground duties at a remote station may be reported as one multi-night booking by ACES.
In this example it is demonstrated that a multi-night layover is mapped to several trip_event records, one per layover,
but that there is only one hotel_booking record representing the entire multi-night booking.
This illustrates a basic multi-night use case where there are only local transport bookings from airport to
the hotel on the day of arrival and from the hotel to the ground duty venue on the day of departure. There are no
additional transports from/to ground duty venues on the rest of the duty days.

### 6.5.5. Multi-night layover with multiple transports

This example demonstrates how multi-night layovers with multiple transport bookings are represented in the data model.
In addition to local transport bookings to/from the hotel on the days of arrival and departure of the multi-night layover,
in this example there are additional transports from/to ground duty venues on intermediate duty days.

Also, in this use case bookings are sent as separate hotel-reservations for each crew member because they have
different pickup times from the hotel. The layover properties and their hotel-reservations are otherwise
identical. In this case there are multiple hotel_booking records created in order to correctly represent the individual
transports and pick-up times.

# 7. Catalog data output

This chapter describes the interface that can be used for extracting catalog data (static data) from JCMS.
Catalog data typically involves enumerations of short names or codes with specific business meaning, for example
codes used for aircraft types, activity types, bases, crew qualifications etc.

The set of codes in the catalog data, and their business meaning, are typically shared between systems exchanging information with JCMS.
Most standard interfaces either provides or requires information matching the catalog data available in JCMS.

The purpose of this interface is to provide external systems, and keep them up to date, with set of catalog data used by JCMS.
The set of catalog data is rather stable, usually loaded once initially and updated only rarely.

Latest version of this interface is 1.beta.
Link to CatalogDataOutput_1_beta.xsd
Link to CatalogDataOutput_1_beta.wsdl
Link to CatalogDataOutput_1_beta_schema.json

Available operations are:

pingPings the service without doing anything (for test purposes).

getAllCatalogDataRequests the full set of catalog data provided by this interface.

## 7.1. Scope of exported data

This interface includes most, but not all, catalog data types in JCMS. See the service definition for full list of data that is exported.
The exported data is provided based on the current state of the catalog data in JCMS, including all values currently available.
The exported data doesn’t contain old, deleted values.
Some values might only be valid for a certain time period.
Such temporal values are always exported together with a validity period, and might not currently be valid.
Some airlines adds additional catalog data types in JCMS database. This interface can be configured for also exporting such airline specific catalog data.

## 7.2. Use cases

The examples below use the plain XML service, the same use cases can be executed in the SOAP service
but then a SOAP envelope and the SoapAction header are required.

The following request is used for requesting the full set of catalog data.

&lt;?xml version=&quot;1.0&quot; encoding=&quot;UTF-8&quot;?&gt;
&lt;getAllCatalogDataRequest xmlns=&quot;http://service.jcms.jeppesen.com/CatalogDataOutput/v1.beta&quot; version=&quot;1.beta&quot; source=&quot;DailyTrigger&quot; created=&quot;2020-06-25T09:31:54Z&quot; /&gt;

All catalog data provided by this interface is included in the response:

# 8. Crew Check-in service

This chapter describes the standard interface for crew member check-in. The service is typically available through
some back-end application where crew members are logged in and authenticated. The back-end application establishes a
session with the Integrator and performs the check-in on behalf of the crew member. The back-end application
itself is not provided by JCMS but is part of a customer solution based on e.g. a smart phone/tablet application or
card reader terminals.

The Crew Check-in is an on-line service. This means that any check-in request is assumed to be issued in conjunction
with the actual duty that the crew member is about to perform. As a consequence, the Crew Check-in service cannot be
used e.g. in a post operational step to register check-in events to JCMS in retrospect.

In JCMS, the Crew Check-in standard interface is a complement to the check-in service available
in Crew Access. In a specific implementation project it may be decided to use this service, the Crew Access
check-in service or a combination of both, depending on the business processes and systems infrastructure available
with the actual airline. In addition to these services there is also a check-in feature available to trackers for
assisted check-in through the Crew Tracking user interface. Using this feature, a tracker may register a check-in
event on behalf of any crew member at any time.

## 8.1. Interface capabilities

The Crew Check-in standard interface supports the following operations:

checkInA request to check in one crew member to a trip. The request always contains the Id of the crew member and a UTC
timestamp when the operation was registered at the client terminal/system. It may also contain an optional airport where
the check-in was taking place. JCMS records the check-in event and returns a response message containing the following
information:

returnCode with success/fail status of the checkIn operation (result of operation: 0=check-in OK, -1=already checked in,
1=check-in failed)

checkInStatus with the crew member’s check-in status after the operation is processed (0=not checked-in, 1=checked in,
2=checked in (assisted))

- a list of unacknowledged notifications that the crew member may have at the time of check-in
- the identity of the trip to which the crew member checks in
- the identity of the first activity of the trip to which the crew member checks in

The JCMS standard version of the checkIn operation first checks the feasibility of the check-in by verifying
that the check-in timestamp is inside a valid time window. The valid check-in time window is defined by business rules
in Rave and may differ between cockpit and cabin crew. If validation fails, a description of the reason for failure is also
provided in the response message.

checkInWithoutValidationIdentical to the ‘checkIn’ operation but without the feasibility checking. Be aware if using this operation that
feasibility checking should instead be implemented on the back-end/client side. At least a validation of the check-in
time window must be implemented and be in accordance with tracking rules in JCMS.

getNotificationsDelivers a list of all unacknowledged notifications for the crew member.

acknowledgeNotificationsA request to acknowledge all unacknowledged notifications for the crew member, if any.

The current version of this interface is 2.
Link to CrewCheckIn_2.xsd
Link to CrewCheckIn_2.wsdl
Link to CrewCheckIn_2_schema.json
Link to CrewCheckIn_2_openapi.json

Previous versions of this interface is 1.0.
Link to CrewCheckIn_1_0.xsd
Link to CrewCheckInSoap_1_0.wsdl

### 8.1.1. Context for check-in

In the standard version of the checkIn operation, the only check done by the system is that check-in is done
within an accepted time frame. No other legality checks are performed as prerequisites for the check-in operation
to succeed. Nor is it checked that the activity to which the crew member checks in actually requires checking in,
or that the role to which he/she is assigned is eligible for check-in. The standard behavior is to look up
the next trip on the crew members roster and verify the accepted check-in time window against the start time
of that trip. Note that check of accepted check-in time window is not performed if using the checkInWithoutValidation
operation.

As for all standard interfaces, the Crew Check-in service is designed to be highly customizable. In particular,
the feasibility check of the checkIn operation is exposed as a Python function that can easily be overridden
and implement any airline specific business level checks and validations. If the validation function returns
a negative result, then the checkIn operation fails.

### 8.1.2. Session handling

A session consistency mechanism is used in JCMS to synchronize the getNotifications and acknowledgeNotifications
operations in order to guarantee that only those notifications are acknowledged that the crew member has
actually seen.

This mechanism utilizes a jcms_state reference header attached to the request message. When set, the IOServer
will make sure that the sub-process that handles the request is based on at least that referenced state (i.e.
the same state or a newer one). The given state is also used as reference point for conflict detection
when storing the acknowledgments to the data model. A data entity level conflict trigger will then cause the
operation to fail if the crew member has more recent notifications in the current state compared to the
ones he/she has viewed. The jcms_state header is set by the IOServer on the getNotifications response
message to the state upon which that operation was based. The same state reference must then follow the
acknowledgeNotifications request message.

There are basically two ways to ensure that the correct jcms_state
reference is attached to the acknowledgeNotifications request. Either the back-end application handles the
state reference or it is handled by the Integrator.

Session handling using integrator

The built-in support in JCMS Integrator for handling
state references can only be used in cases where the front-end client only handles one crew member
per session. Each client must authenticate it self, i.e. by logging in using the crew member ID to initiate the session.

Session handling using back-end client

If instead the back-end application handles requests on behalf of many crew members, and using a
stateless session for the communication with JCMS, then the back-end application itself must handle the jcms_state
references for each front-end client. In this case it is required that acknowledgeNotifications request for a crew member
contains the jcms_state reference previously received in the getNotifications response for that crew member,
i.e. the back-end application must handle jcms_state references separately per crew member.
Also note that the conflict trigger mentioned above is not included in
the standard JCMS data model but must be added as part of a CARMUSR implementation.

In the standard version of the Crew Check-in service, no synchronization is required between acknowledgeNotifications
and checkIn though because check-in should succeed regardless if there are unacknowledged notifications.
For that reason, the conflict trigger mentioned above is not active when saving the result of the checkIn
operation.
One way to enforce acknowledgement before check-in, is simply that the back-end application never sends
a checkIn request before receiving the response from a successful acknowledgeNotifications operation. Also,
the registered check-in timestamp should be set to the time of the acknowledgeNotifications request or
earlier, e.g. the time when the crew member logged in to the back-end application.

### 8.1.3. Supported protocols

The interface supports requests using SOAP or plain xml. The service itself doesn’t implement the actual communication
protocol. As a part of a customer solution it typically relies on the JEE based Integrator to expose the
service over HTTP.

## 8.2. Rave definitions

The following Rave variables are defined in the CARMSYS and used by the Crew Check-in standard interface:

- interfaces_core.%start_of_check_in_time_window_utc%
- interfaces_core.%end_of_check_in_time_window_utc%
- interfaces_core.%leg_requires_check_in%
- interfaces_core.%crew_is_checked_in%
- interfaces_core.%crew_checked_in_time%
- interfaces_core.%is_assisted_check_in%

The business logic behind these Rave variables need to be implemented in a CARMUSR to comply with the
expected behavior of each individual airline. Note that the start_of_check_in_time_window_utc is per
definition included in the valid check-in time window whereas the end_of_check_in_time_window_utc
is excluded.

## 8.3. Error Handling

When a checkIn operation fails due to a validation error, an ordinary checkInResponse message is returned
but with returnCode set to 1, and the errorDescription field containing detailed information about the
actual validation error. In the standard Crew Check-in interface, the only validation that is actually
carried out is to check that the check-in timestamp is inside a valid time window.

All other kinds of errors will result in an error message (of type ServiceError). See following
sub-sections for details.

### 8.3.1. Check-in validation errors

Error

Response message type

returnCode

errorDescription

Check-in too early

CheckInResponseMsg

1

Check-in time ‘DDMONYYYY hh:MM’ is outside
valid time window (DDMONYYYY hh:MM - DDMONYYYY hh:MM)

Check-in too late

CheckInResponseMsg

1

Check-in time ‘DDMONYYYY hh:MM’ is outside
valid time window (DDMONYYYY hh:MM - DDMONYYYY hh:MM)

## 8.4. Detailed use cases

### 8.4.1. Acknowledge notifications for crew member and verify

Client sends initial getNotificationsRequest for crew member 12345A.
The HTTP header of the initial request for this crew member must contain jcms_state=0.

	&lt;/SOAP:Body&gt;
&lt;/SOAP:Envelope&gt;

Service responds with three notifications for crew member 12345A.
The HTTP header of the response for this crew member contains jcms_state=325.

the three notifications previously received for this crew member are acknowledged.
